 Advertisment Indian Markets What's the Biggest Problem Cigarette Companies in India Are Facing?
 India’s cigarette industry faces growing pressure from higher taxes, rising illicit trade, and declining legal sales, forcing major companies like ITC and Godfrey Phillips to protect profitability and market share.
 by Nikhil Naik by Nikhil Naik 
 10 Nov 2026 14:00 IST
 Link copied! Copy failed! India's cigarette industry is facing a difficult business environment, and the biggest concern is no longer just rising taxes. Higher taxation is also creating an opportunity for illegal cigarette sellers, putting pressure on legal manufacturers such as ITC and Godfrey Phillips India. As cigarette prices increase, companies are finding it harder to protect sales volumes, maintain profit margins, and compete with cheaper smuggled products. 
 Advertisment The latest financial updates for the first half of FY27 highlight the pressure. Godfrey Phillips India reported a 41 percent year-on-year decline in net profit, while ITC said legal cigarette industry volumes remained under pressure. These developments highlight a growing problem for the cigarette industry: companies are paying higher taxes and facing weaker profitability, while illegal products are becoming a more serious competitive threat.

 Higher Taxes Have Become the Biggest Challenge for Cigarette Companies 
 The sharp increase in cigarette taxation has changed the business environment for India's cigarette manufacturers. From February 1, 2026, cigarettes came under a 40 percent GST rate along with additional excise duty based on cigarette length. This has increased the tax burden on manufacturers and pushed up prices for consumers.  
 Advertisment For cigarette companies, passing the entire tax increase to consumers can make cigarettes more expensive and affect demand. This is particularly challenging in a price-sensitive market like India, where consumers may look for cheaper alternatives when prices rise. At the same time, absorbing a larger part of the tax burden can reduce the company's margins and profitability. 
 Godfrey Phillips India management highlighted this issue in its H1 FY27 earnings presentation. CEO Sharad Aggarwal said the steep tax increase had affected industry profitability and contributed to the growth of illicit trade. The company has adopted a calibrated pricing strategy to contain the impact on volumes while continuing to invest in brands, innovation, and operational efficiency. 
 This shows that taxation is no longer just a regulatory expense for cigarette manufacturers. It has become a major factor influencing their pricing decisions, market share, and future profitability.  
 Advertisment Illegal and Smuggled Cigarettes Are Becoming a Bigger Threat 
 The second major problem is the growing presence of illegal and smuggled cigarettes in the Indian market. 
 Legal cigarette manufacturers operate under government regulations and pay applicable GST and excise duties. However, illegal cigarette sellers avoid these taxes and can offer products at comparatively lower prices. This creates an uneven competitive environment for companies operating within the legal system. 
 When the price difference between legal and illegal cigarettes becomes wider, consumers looking for cheaper products may become more attracted to smuggled alternatives. This puts established manufacturers under additional pressure because they must compete with products that do not carry the same tax costs. 
 Advertisment ITC highlighted this concern in its November 2026 media statement. The company reported a sharp increase in seizures of smuggled cigarette consignments by enforcement agencies across India. According to its management, the widening tax difference is creating opportunities for unscrupulous players and anti-social elements. ITC is responding by introducing new product variants and strengthening its own trademarks with international appeal to compete with global smuggled brands. 
 Profitability Is Falling Despite Higher Sales 
 Another major challenge is the pressure on profitability. Higher cigarette prices and tax collections can increase reported sales values, but this does not necessarily mean companies are earning more money. 
 Godfrey Phillips India's H1 FY27 financial performance provides a clear example. The company reported consolidated gross sales of Rs. 11,929 crore, compared with Rs. 8,068 crore in the corresponding period last year. However, its net profit declined to Rs. 388.29 crore from Rs. 661.27 crore, representing a fall of approximately 41 percent. Its gross profit also declined by 23.6 percent to Rs. 937 crore, while its gross profit margin reduced to 36.8 percent from 44.2 percent in H1 FY26 
 ITC is also experiencing pressure in its cigarette business. According to its Q2 FY27 results, cigarette segment revenue increased in reported terms, partly reflecting the higher tax component, but net cigarette revenue declined by 21 percent year on year. Cigarette segment profit also fell by 27.2 percent to Rs. 3,813 crore in the quarter.  
 These figures show why higher reported sales values do not necessarily translate into better financial performance. Companies must manage the additional tax burden while protecting their underlying earnings. 
 Pressure on the Entire Tobacco Supply Chain 
 The problem is not limited to cigarette manufacturers. It also affects tobacco farmers, suppliers, distributors, and other businesses connected to the industry. 
 ITC mentioned that lower domestic demand following the tax increase continues to affect its overall leaf tobacco business. It also warned that the significant reduction in the FCV tobacco crop size announced by the Tobacco Board could affect Indian tobacco farmers' earnings and livelihoods.

 Godfrey Phillips India is also looking towards international markets to strengthen its tobacco business. During H1 FY27, its unmanufactured tobacco exports generated Rs 591 crore, contributing 7 percent of net sales revenue. However, management noted that geopolitical factors had affected exports. 
 How Are ITC and Godfrey Phillips India Responding? 
 Despite these challenges, cigarette manufacturers are not simply waiting for market conditions to improve. They are changing their business strategies to protect profitability, retain consumers, and compete more effectively. 
 ITC is focusing on calibrated pricing, portfolio restructuring, and stronger trademarks. It is also introducing new variants to strengthen its market position and compete with smuggled international brands. The company reported an improvement in its quarter-on-quarter cigarette business performance, although legal industry volumes remain under pressure. 
 Godfrey Phillips India is focusing on brand investments, product innovation, market execution, and operational efficiencies. Its future priorities include strengthening its partnership with Philip Morris International for Marlboro cigarettes, improving distribution efficiency, and expanding international tobacco exports. 
 Godfrey Phillips reported Rs 78 crore in gross sales from other consumer products in H1 FY27, while its tobacco business accounted for approximately 99 percent of gross sales value. 
 These developments show why companies are trying to strengthen other business segments while protecting their core cigarette operations. However, diversification cannot immediately remove the financial pressure created by weaker cigarette profitability. 
 What Lies Ahead for India's Cigarette Industry? 
 The future of the cigarette industry will depend largely on three factors: taxation, enforcement against illegal trade, and the ability of companies to maintain consumer demand. 
 Manufacturers will need to balance pricing decisions with profitability while improving their competitiveness in the legal market. Stronger action against smuggling will also be important in addressing the price advantage enjoyed by illegal sellers.

 The latest results from ITC and Godfrey Phillips India suggest that the impact of higher taxation is already significant. Both companies are changing their strategies, but the pressure on profitability and legal cigarette volumes remains. 
 Ultimately, the biggest problem facing cigarette companies in India is the combination of higher taxation and growing illicit trade. Higher taxes are squeezing margins and making legal products more expensive, while illegal sellers are gaining a pricing advantage. Until this imbalance is addressed, protecting sales volumes and restoring profitability will remain major challenges for India's cigarette manufacturers.
